concept.body: Two forms of the same rule. TEST: three lengths form a triangle iff the two shortest sum to MORE than the longest. RANGE: given two sides a and b, the third must satisfy |a − b| < third < a + b. Greater than the difference, less than the sum.

explanationVariants: Check the two shortest: 2 + 3 = 5, which is NOT more than 6 — so no triangle.
2 + 3 = 5 < 6 fails the inequality; these can't form a triangle.

widget.prompt: Can sides 2, 3, and 6 form a triangle?

options.label: No — 2 + 3 = 5, which is less than 6
options.feedback: The two shortest sides fall short of the longest, so no triangle forms.

options.label: Yes — all sides are different
options.feedback: Different lengths don't guarantee a triangle; here 2 + 3 < 6 fails the inequality.

options.label: Yes — 6 is the longest
options.feedback: Having a longest side is fine, but 2 + 3 = 5 can't reach across 6. No triangle.

options.label: Only if it's a right triangle
options.feedback: Right or not, 2 + 3 < 6 means the sides can't close into any triangle.

steps.body: Not every trio of lengths makes a triangle. The **Triangle Inequality** says the sum of any two sides must **exceed** the third. If two sides can't reach across the gap left by the third, they never meet — the triangle collapses flat or fails entirely. Check all three pairings to be safe.

widget.prompt: Sort each set of three lengths: can they form a triangle?

items.feedback: 3 + 4 = 7 > 5, and the other pairs work too — a valid triangle (in fact right).
2 + 3 = 5, far short of 10 — the two short sides can't reach across. No triangle.
5 + 6 = 11 > 7, and all pairings exceed the third — valid.
4 + 4 = 8 < 9 — the two equal sides fall short of the long one. No triangle.

widget.missFeedback: For each set, check that the two SHORTEST sides sum to MORE than the longest.
widget.successFeedback: Two shortest must outreach the longest.

explanationVariants: You only need to check that the two SHORTEST sides sum to more than the longest — if that holds, all three pairings do.
The tightest pairing is the two small sides vs the big one; pass that and the triangle exists.

widget.prompt: What's the fastest way to test whether three lengths form a triangle?

options.label: Check that the two shortest sides sum to more than the longest
options.feedback: The two smallest summing past the largest is the hardest condition — if it holds, the triangle is valid.

options.label: Check that the two longest sides sum to more than the shortest
options.feedback: That's the EASIEST pairing and almost always passes — it doesn't catch failures. Test the two SHORTEST vs the longest.

options.label: Add all three sides and compare to 180
options.feedback: 180 is about ANGLES, not side lengths. Compare the two shortest sides' sum to the longest side.

options.label: Check that all three sides are equal
options.feedback: Triangles needn't be equilateral. The test is the two shortest sides exceeding the longest.

steps.body: The inequality also **bounds the third side**. Given two sides, the third must be more than their **difference** and less than their **sum**: |a − b| < third < a + b. Too short and the sides overlap; too long and they can't close. That window is exactly the buildable range.

widget.prompt: Sides 5 and 8 are fixed. Drag the third side as far as it will go — note where it stops — then bring it to where the angle facing it reads exactly 60°.
widget.successFeedback: A third side of 7, with the angle opposite it at exactly 60°. The more important reading is where the dial ran out: it stops at 12, because at 13 the two short sides would lie flat along the third and enclose nothing. That is the upper bound — the third side must be LESS than 5 + 8, and the triangle stops existing rather than merely looking wrong.
widget.lowFeedback: The angle opposite the third side is still under 60°, which means the third side is too short. Lengthen it — and notice the two fixed sides opening apart as you do.
widget.highFeedback: The angle has gone past 60°, so the third side is too long. Shorten it. Keep pushing the other way and you will meet the dial's ceiling, which is the inequality itself.

predict.prompt: Two sides measure 5 and 8. As you stretch the third side longer and longer, the triangle will…

options.label: Stop existing once the third side reaches 13
Keep existing, just getting flatter forever
Exist for any third side at all

predict.reveal: It stops. At exactly 13 the sides 5 and 8 lie flat end to end along the third side, enclosing no area at all, and beyond that they cannot reach. The bound is not a rule bolted onto triangles — it is the point where two sides can no longer meet.

explanationVariants: The third side must exceed the DIFFERENCE of the other two: 8 − 5 = 3.
Lower bound is |a − b| = |8 − 5| = 3; the third side must be greater than 3.

widget.prompt: With two sides 5 and 8, the third side must be GREATER than what value?

commonErrors.feedback: 13 is the UPPER bound (5 + 8) — the third must be LESS than that. The lower bound is the DIFFERENCE: 8 − 5 = 3.
0 is too weak — a side of length 2 would fail (2 + 5 < 8). The real floor is |8 − 5| = 3.

steps.body: Sides and angles line up in order: the **largest angle sits opposite the largest side**, the smallest opposite the smallest. So in a 5-6-7 triangle, the biggest angle faces the 7. This side-angle ranking lets you order a triangle's angles just by glancing at its sides.

widget.prompt: In a triangle with sides 5, 6, and 7, which side is the largest angle opposite to?

options.label: the side of length 7
options.feedback: The largest angle always sits opposite the largest side — here that's the 7.

options.label: the side of length 5
options.feedback: The 5 is the SMALLEST side, so it faces the SMALLEST angle. The largest angle is opposite the 7.

options.label: the side of length 6
options.feedback: The 6 is the middle side, facing the middle angle. The largest angle is opposite the longest side, 7.

options.label: they are all equal
options.feedback: The sides differ (5, 6, 7), so the angles differ too — the largest faces the 7.

hints: Two sides are 7 and 10. What's the range for the third side?
The third side must satisfy 10 − 7 < x < 10 + 7, i.e. 3 < x < 17.
Count the INTEGER values strictly between 3 and 17.
explanationVariants: The third side satisfies 3 < x < 17, so integer values run 4, 5, …, 16 — that's 13 values.
Integers strictly between 3 and 17 are 4 through 16 inclusive: 16 − 4 + 1 = 13.

widget.prompt: Two sides of a triangle are 7 and 10. How many INTEGER values are possible for the third side?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 counts 3 through 16 — but the third side must be strictly GREATER than 3, so start at 4: values 4..16 = 13.
17 is the upper bound itself, which is excluded. Integers strictly between 3 and 17 are 4..16 = 13.

takeaways: Triangle Inequality: any two sides must sum to more than the third.
Third side is bounded: |a − b| < third < a + b.
Largest angle sits opposite the largest side.
steps.teaser: Next: fix two sides and open the angle between them — the hinge theorem.
